findings.title: Give each fact one value and one wording everywhere it appears
findings.evidence: One paragraph says 'we show what we accomplished after spending the majority of our Series A $4.7MM financing'. Two later paragraphs say 'we spent the $4 million from our Series A' and 'LinkedIn had spent its $4 milli[on]'. The page gives the same round as $4.7 million once and $4 million twice, and says 'the majority of' it was spent once and all of it twice.
findings.before: 'our Series A $4.7MM financing' … 'we spent the $4 million from our Series A'
findings.after: One figure for the Series A everywhere, stated once with its date, and the later mentions worded to match ('most of the Series A').
findings.why: The essay asks readers to trust its numbers as a case study. Two amounts for one round make a reader doubt the other figures in the deck.

findings.title: Dates are current and true
findings.evidence: The intro says 'This past May was the 10th anniversary of LinkedIn', and the page shows no publication date. Later it says 'When you compare that to our current public market prices' and 'Today in 2013 …', while the footer reads 'Reid Hoffman © 2026'. A reader in 2026 meets 'this past May' and 'current' with no year until the 2013 aside.
findings.before: This past May was the 10th anniversary of LinkedIn … our current public market prices
findings.after: Put the publication date under the title (for example 'Published June 2013'), or write the year into the relative phrases ('In May 2013, LinkedIn turned ten').
findings.why: The '© 2026' footer makes the essay look current, so 'current public market prices' can read as a claim about today rather than about 2013.
